# tScrub — Compliance-Grade Erasure, Triage & Grading

tScrub is an open ITAD (IT asset disposition) platform built for compliance. One boot erases its NVMe, SATA, and SCSI drives to NIST 800-88 Clear, Purge, and Destroy levels and produces a signed chain-of-custody report you can turn into a Certificate of Destruction — while it also captures the machine's full hardware profile (display panel, battery health and capacity, CPU spec, memory modules, storage, firmware, and MDM or BIOS lock status) and grades it for resale, redeployment, or recycling, with a printable two-page ITAD diagnostics report. The bootable appliance image is open and inspectable — your security team can read every line of what runs. Boot it from USB or PXE on hardware you already own. No locked-down vendor box required.

## What it does

- **NVMe sanitise** — crypto, block, and overwrite sanitise, plus format fallback, with live SSTAT progress monitoring.
- **ATA secure erase** — enhanced and standard security erase for SATA/ATA drives, with frozen-drive handling.
- **SCSI sanitise** — for SAS/SCSI drives.
- **SED / OPAL unlock** — PSID revert for locked self-encrypting drives, plus detection of BIOS Block SID lockdown (0x4286).
- **Chain of custody** — COCID, system serials, and per-drive final status in a single CSV report for the whole job.
- **SMART capture** — pre/post-wipe SMART health (status, temperature, power-on hours, wear) recorded per drive.
- **Post-erasure verification** — before erasing, a per-run sentinel is written to five fixed positions (start, 25%, 50%, 75%, end); after the wipe those sectors are re-read and must be gone (sampled by default, full re-read opt-in). The result is recorded per drive, together with the *technique* that produced it: `sentinel` (the check above), `overwrite-sample` (N% of the address space read back and found zero, only after a software overwrite, opt-in via `--verify-coverage N`), or `ce-exempt` (a crypto erase destroyed the media key, so a content read-back proves nothing either way). A firmware erase always records `sentinel` and never a coverage percentage.
- **Opt-in sanitisation-standard claim** — reports name the technique and the evidence by default, and claim no standard. With `tscrub_standard=ieee2883` (or `--standard ieee2883`) each drive is tested against five gates and labelled `IEEE 2883-2022` only where all pass: the technique must map to a real 2883 method and reach non-addressable locations to claim `Purge` (an ATA *normal* erase and an NVMe Format reach only the addressable area, so they are `Clear`); Clear on the software-overwrite path needs a read-back sample of at least 5% (house policy, not a quoted requirement); the sentinel must be gone, with a crypto erase exempt by design and the exemption recorded; the erase must have completed; and only HDD, SATA SSD, NVMe and SAS carry the claim. A refused drive keeps `NIST 800-88` and records the failing gate in `SanitizationShortfall` (for example `G2 coverage 2% < 5%`), so a refusal is machine-readable. The achieved level is recorded per drive as `SanitizationLevel` (`Clear` / `Purge`), and the certificate's `Standard` row names the standard only when every scored drive earned it, printing the levels: `IEEE 2883-2022 (Clear, Purge)`. tScrub is not certified to IEEE 2883 and no third party has audited it against that standard, exactly as nothing is "NIST 800-88 certified"; certificates therefore print "IEEE 2883-2022 methods described, not IEEE certified". The claim asserts only that these methods were used and this evidence captured per drive. Default is `nist` and unchanged.
- **Air-gapped certificate verification** — the certificate QR opens `tscrub.com/verify-offline` with a signed code in the URL fragment, so the code is never sent to the server. The code is a pipe-separated message `2|tscrub-vendor-1|<cert_id>|<issued_at>|<ed25519 signature>`: the format version, key ID, Certificate ID and issue timestamp are signed with the tScrub vendor key, which is pinned in the page and published at `/.well-known/tscrub-cert-key.json`. The caption under the QR tells you which generation you hold: "Verify offline or online" (signed code, issued from 21 Oct 2026) or "Verify online" (record link `tscrub.com/verify?cert=…`, used by older certificates and whenever the vendor key was unavailable at generation). It attests issuance and integrity only: it does not attest which drives were erased, and it deliberately carries no customer name, serials or PDF hash. The page verifies an Ed25519 signature on the device against a pinned key (fingerprint published at `/.well-known/tscrub-cert-key.json`), and keeps working with no network once loaded. It proves the certificate was issued by tScrub for that Certificate ID at that time and has not been altered; the recorded drive-level content stays a matter for the online record.
- **HPA/DCO hidden-area removal** — Host Protected Area and Device Configuration Overlay hidden areas are reset to the native size before erasing, so the full native capacity is sanitised, not just the visible capacity.
- **Verifiable proof of destruction** — reports can be signed (SHA-256 + Ed25519), producing a sidecar signature and manifest that auditors can independently verify.
- **Machine-readable certificates** — every Certificate of Destruction is also issued as a signed JSON-LD document (add `&format=jsonld` to the verification URL) with a detached Ed25519 signature and an RFC 3161 timestamp, so compliance platforms and LLM auditors can ingest and verify it without parsing the PDF.
- **Attested destruction for assets that never ran tScrub** — phones and tablets with soldered storage, machines that will not power on or boot, sealed units, and media a wipe cannot address at all can be recorded by hand (the Add button on the Devices and Media pages): type or category, make, model, serial (typically an IMEI for a phone), the reason it was destroyed rather than sanitised (from a controlled list: would not power on, would not boot / no supported interface, media soldered / integrated, unsupported media type, battery unsafe to power, physically damaged, beyond economic repair, other), the destruction method (shredded, crushed, degaussed, incinerated, disintegrated, dismantled then shredded, other), and optionally the vendor, date, a witness and the vendor's own evidence reference. The attester is taken from the signed-in account, never from the form. Recording is free. These items join the same Chain of Custody as machine-wiped drives so one job yields one certificate, where they appear in their own section with every line qualified "operator-attested — not instrument-verified". They are never described as sanitised and carry no wipe result, NIST SP 800-88 level or pre/post-wipe SMART data, because none was ever observed. Identity is the normalised serial + make + model, unique within the job; a genuine duplicate asks the operator to assign an asset tag so two identical units stay distinguishable. In the dashboard they are badged Attested and counted separately, so attested items cannot inflate the figure for machines the appliance actually saw.
- **Media removed from an asset and erased on a bench machine** — storage that will not erase in its own chassis (a failing drive, a firmware erase the controller refuses, or media that was already pulled) can be erased on another machine. The erasure stays instrument-verified wherever it ran; the certificate also states where the medium came from. Provenance is derived automatically where the appliance observed the medium (the asset's boot snapshot, or a FAILED/BLOCKED/FROZEN erasure row under that asset's serial) and is otherwise recorded by the operator on the Media page as a declared origin, labelled "declared by operator" and never presented as instrument-verified. Annex A gains an ASSET ACCOUNTING block for media removed and sanitised on a different host, assets with no data-bearing media at intake, and assets whose media did not complete; it adds an Origin asset column beside Machine SN only when the two differ. The certificate never says a device was sanitised in place when only its media were. A bench machine is marked as a processing host from its Ops panel, excluded from the customer's fleet and certificate asset counts while its evidence is still used. The JSON-LD twin carries `originAsset` / `originProvenance` / `hostSerial` per drive and an `assetAccounting` block.
- **Hardware triage & grading** — boot-time capture of the display panel (manufacturer, resolution, diagonal size, year), battery (health and full-charge capacity in Wh, cycle count), CPU core/thread spec, DIMM part numbers, board serial, SKU/asset tag, BIOS vendor/version, TPM, Secure Boot, MAC addresses, and storage controllers.
- **MDM check, BIOS lock report & unlock** — the machine's hardware hash is captured with its diagnostics report and BIOS password-lock detection is recorded at boot; the Windows Autopilot MDM check (Locked/Unlocked) is run from the device's page in the dashboard. Remote commands can be dispatched from the dashboard — shut down, restart, stage a wipe, or clear a BIOS admin password on supported Dell, Lenovo and HP machines (including HP Setup Passwords cleared from Linux over the firmware's own interface); when a clear fails the dashboard states why, and every command is recorded in a per-device log stamped with the chain of custody of the session that ran it.
- **Printable diagnostics report** — each device snapshot renders as a two-page ITAD triage PDF (machine summary + storage inventory), downloadable from the Devices tab.
- **Hardware self-tests (opt-in)** — a deterministic CPU arithmetic check plus a per-drive short self-test (SMART for SATA, NVMe device-self-test for NVMe).
- **Audit-proof report identity** — every report carries a report_id (UUID) and a digital_identifier (SHA-256 over the snapshot), making each report individually identifiable and tamper-evident.

## How it works (four steps)

1. **Boot** — boot the tScrub appliance image from USB or PXE and run it; tScrub needs zero installation.
2. **Triage & grade** — tScrub connects to the network, submits its diagnostics, records the machine's full hardware profile (display, battery, CPU, RAM, storage, MDM and BIOS lock status), and starts an online heartbeat while showing the triage screen.
3. **Erase (Shift+T)** — press Shift+T to pick drives and erase them, with live progress; frozen and blocked drives are flagged. The heartbeat keeps running throughout and after.
4. **Report** — a printable ITAD diagnostics report plus a chain-of-custody CSV with method, certification, final status, and pre/post-wipe SMART per drive.

## Compliance

- Maps each wipe method to NIST 800-88 Clear, Purge, and Destroy outcomes.
- Chain-of-custody reporting supports GDPR, HIPAA, and ISO 27001 programmes.
- Financial services (FCA/PRA), healthcare (UK GDPR/NHS), ITAD & refurbishers, and data centres are primary audiences.

## Comparison vs Blancco

tScrub is the open, auditable alternative to Blancco for ITAD — erasure plus hardware grading, MDM/BIOS lock detection, and a printable diagnostics report, with the same NIST 800-88 sanitisation outcomes and no vendor lock-in.

| Capability | tScrub | Blancco |
|---|---|---|
| Source & auditability | Open, inspectable (GPL-3.0) | Closed, proprietary |
| NVMe / SATA / SCSI erasure | Native firmware purge | Yes |
| NIST 800-88 outcome mapping | Built in (Clear / Purge / Destroy) | Yes |
| Runs on your own hardware | Yes (boot USB or PXE) | Licensed software |
| Chain-of-custody report | Signed CSV + JSON + hashes, built in | Platform |
| Certificate of Destruction | PDF, self-serve, QR-verified, signed JSON-LD | Platform |
| Pre/post-wipe SMART capture | Built in | Platform |
| Self-serve accounts & licences | Free tier, self-serve | Enterprise quote |
| Hardware triage & grading (display, battery, CPU, RAM) | Built in | Platform |
| MDM & BIOS lock detection | Built in | Platform |
| Printable diagnostics report | Built in | Platform |
| Pricing | Transparent | Enterprise quote |

The key differences: tScrub is open and inspectable — every line of the erasure code is auditable — while Blancco is closed. tScrub generates the chain-of-custody report and the signed Certificate of Destruction itself (CSV + JSON manifest + PDF with a verification QR, plus a signed machine-readable JSON-LD twin); Blancco routes both through its proprietary platform. tScrub also captures a full hardware profile and MDM/BIOS lock status in the same boot and renders a printable diagnostics report, so a single tool covers triage, grading, and erasure. tScrub has a self-serve free tier and transparent per-device pricing; Blancco is enterprise-quote only.

### vs free wipe tools (nwipe / DBAN)

nwipe and DBAN are a different class: free, ad-hoc overwrite tools with no signed reports, no certificates, and no NIST 800-88 outcome mapping. nwipe is actually bundled inside tScrub as the SCSI/SAS software-overwrite fallback (mapped to Clear) — it is a component of tScrub, not a competitor. The fallback can run a named standard — `zero`, `random` (PRNG stream), `dod` (DoD 5220.22-M), `dodshort` (DoD Short), `gutmann` (Gutmann), `is5enh` (HMG IS5 Enhanced) — with `--passes N`, and the report records the standard (`OverwriteStandard`), the
pass count and the engine version. The standard is chosen on the appliance itself (on the triage screen, `m` cycles the standard and `p` cycles the rounds, and the footer shows the resulting number of pattern passes), from the kernel command line (`tscrub_method=`, `tscrub_passes=`), or from the CLI (`--method`, `--passes`). It applies to the software-overwrite fallback only: a drive whose firmware erase is available is never overwritten, and an overwrite is always recorded as Clear, never Purge. DBAN is effectively unmaintained and only overwrites hard drives. tScrub is the upgrade path from both: firmware-level purge for NVMe/SSD plus a signed, verifiable chain of custody.

## Pricing & download

- **Free tier** — full erasure with self-signed reports (tamper-evident, not attributable); a free licence is required.
- **Pay-as-you-go** — prepaid credit packs from £1.80 per device (10 for £27, 50 for £112.50, 100 for £180) for attributable reports (signed and licence-verified).
- **Team** — £99 one-off for 100 credits, attributable reports and priority support; includes a shared organisation with up to 50 seats.
- **Enterprise** — £399 one-off for 500 credits, for regulated fleets; includes a shared organisation with up to 100 seats.
- The Windows Autopilot (MDM) lock check is a paid feature — one credit per live check, from the same balance.
- Team and Enterprise organisations share one workspace — devices, reports, certificates, remote-command queues and a pooled credit balance — across their seats (2 on Free, 10 on Pay-as-you-go, 50 on Team, 100 on Enterprise).

See pricing at https://tscrub.com/pricing and download the appliance image at https://tscrub.com/download. Free licences are self-serve; paid tiers are issued by the tScrub team.

## Getting started

Step-by-step documentation is at https://tscrub.com/docs. Download the bootable appliance ISO from the public Download page (https://tscrub.com/download) and issue your licence from your dashboard Licences page (account required). Boot the tScrub appliance image from USB or PXE and run it. At the end of a run the appliance writes the report locally (boot USB, or `tscrub_output=`) and can push it to your dashboard (`tscrub_api_token=`) or FTP/SFTP (`tscrub_output=ftp:…` / `tscrub_output=sftp:…`). Reports are verified automatically when uploaded to the dashboard, and certificates verify online via their QR code.

## Certificate of Destruction

The end-to-end loop is: boot → triage (diagnostics + online heartbeat) → Shift+T erase → signed chain-of-custody report → Certificate of Destruction, verifiable at every step. The customer (the data controller) certifies their own destruction — tScrub provides the signed, tamper-evident evidence.

Upload a tScrub report (CSV + JSON manifest + optional signature) on the dashboard Reports page, then select its Chain of Custody ID on the Certificates page to generate a printable PDF Certificate of Destruction. Every certificate states on page 1 **how the data was destroyed** — the method, the NIST SP 800-88 level reached (Clear / Purge / Destruction), the technique (for example cryptographic erase, where the media encryption key is destroyed) and the media disposition ("N media sanitised in place (data destroyed; hardware reusable); M media physically destroyed") — and the outcome banner reads "DATA DESTROYED ON ALL N DEVICE(S)". Assets that never ran the appliance can be added by hand (see attested destruction above) and are shown in their own section under the qualifier "operator-attested — not instrument-verified", never as sanitised evidence. Annex A opens with a DESTRUCTION METHOD SUMMARY (one line per method: label, level, technique, device count) and then lists every drive; the signed JSON-LD twin carries the same evidence as `sanitizationTechnique` / `nistLevel` per drive and `mediaDisposition` at chain level. Certificates include a device annex (Annex A), a pre/post-wipe SMART capture annex (Annex B, when present in the report: status, temperature, power-on hours, wear), and a verification QR code on every certificate. The QR encodes tscrub.com/verify?cert=COD-…, which confirms the issuance record and document hash; on free-tier certificates the same scan explains that the certificate is self-signed and cannot be independently confirmed, with an upgrade prompt to a commercial plan for attributable verification. Generated certificates are listed on the Certificates page for download and management.

## SMART data reports

Per-medium erasure and pre/post-wipe SMART data for every uploaded report are available at tscrub.com/dashboard/drives: device, type, model, serial, sanitisation method, certification, final status, and before/after SMART attributes (status, temperature, power-on hours, power cycles, wear, TBW).

## Hardware triage & the Devices dashboard

Every machine that boots tScrub registers itself and appears at tscrub.com/dashboard/devices with a full hardware profile captured at boot: system and board serials, SKU and asset tag, BIOS vendor/version, motherboard, TPM status, Secure Boot state, CPU core/thread spec, per-DIMM memory (size/type/speed/serial/part number), the internal display panel (manufacturer, resolution, diagonal size, manufacture year from EDID), the Wi-Fi adapter model, and battery (model, serial, charge, health, full-charge capacity in Wh, cycle count). Per-drive health — firmware revision, logical sector size, SMART health, most recent self-test result, reallocated-sector count, and HPA/DCO and SED/OPAL lock state — is captured alongside the machine profile. The dashboard also shows each machine's online/offline presence and its LAN IP, and each device's snapshot renders as a printable two-page ITAD triage report PDF. Opt-in hardware self-tests add a CPU arithmetic check and a per-drive short self-test. From the dashboard you can also power a machine off or restart it remotely, stage a remote wipe, clear a BIOS admin password on supported Dell, Lenovo and HP machines, and organise Team/Enterprise seats into a shared organisation with a pooled credit balance. Each device has a log of every recorded event, and each remote command is stamped with the chain of custody of the session that ran it.

  - **Block SID lockdown** (https://tscrub.com/resources/block-sid) — what NVMe error 0x4286 means.
- **Wipe methods** (https://tscrub.com/resources/wipe-methods) — firmware vs software erasure, Secure vs Enhanced Erase, sanitise vs format, crypto vs block erase, overwrite limits, and degaussing.
  - **Secure Erase vs Enhanced Secure Erase** (https://tscrub.com/resources/secure-vs-enhanced-erase) — Clear vs Purge, reallocated sectors.
  - **Crypto erase vs block erase** (https://tscrub.com/resources/crypto-vs-block-erase) — the two Purge-level NVMe Sanitize modes.
  - **Software overwrite** (https://tscrub.com/resources/software-overwrite) — how it works and its limits (nwipe/dd).
  - **Degaussing & physical destruction** (https://tscrub.com/resources/degaussing-destruction) — when erasure isn't possible.
- **Certificates & chain of custody** (https://tscrub.com/resources/certificates) — what a certificate of destruction is, what it must include, the verification QR code, and free vs paid signing.  - **Chain of custody** (https://tscrub.com/resources/chain-of-custody) — the per-drive record, COCIDs.

  - **How to verify a certificate** (https://tscrub.com/resources/verify-certificate) — the QR code, the offline signed-code check, and /verify.
  - **SMART data as audit evidence** (https://tscrub.com/resources/smart-audit-evidence) — pre/post-wipe health.- **Buyer's guide** (https://tscrub.com/resources/buyers-guide) — choosing data erasure software, tScrub vs Blancco, and ITAD / data-centre considerations.
  - **DBAN alternatives** (https://tscrub.com/resources/dban-alternatives) — modern options that handle SSDs and NVMe.
  - **Open source vs commercial** (https://tscrub.com/resources/open-source-vs-commercial) — transparency vs certification.
